claims.text: A multicolumn B-tree index orders its entries by the first column, then by the next column among entries with equal earlier values.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 11.3 Multicolumn Indexes; 11.4 Indexes and ORDER BY

claims.text: A multicolumn B-tree index is most efficient with constraints on the leading column(s): equality on the leading column plus a range on the next column limits the portion of the index scanned; a condition on a later column alone does not reduce the portion scanned (PostgreSQL 17 has no skip scan).
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 11.3 Multicolumn Indexes ('the leading (leftmost) columns ... constraints on columns to the right ... do not reduce the portion of the index that has to be scanned')

claims.text: A B-tree index can deliver rows in its sort order, so a query with ORDER BY matching the index order (after equality on the leading column) needs no separate Sort step, and with LIMIT the scan stops after the requested rows.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 11.4 Indexes and ORDER BY ('especially useful with ORDER BY combined with LIMIT n')

claims.text: PostgreSQL can combine several indexes (bitmap AND/OR) to find matching rows, but then visits the table rows in physical order, losing the indexes' ordering, so an ORDER BY needs a separate sort.

At stage-2, DonHangDbContext declares e.HasIndex(o => new { o.CustomerId, o.Id }) on Order; migration ReplaceOrdersCustomerIdIndex drops IX_orders_customer_id and creates IX_orders_customer_id_id on (customer_id, id).
Once an index starting with customer_id exists in the model, EF Core does not create its own foreign key index for CustomerId (covered), which is why the migration drops IX_orders_customer_id.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Modeling > Relationships > Conventions, 'Indexes' NOTE (already covered by an existing index); ReplaceOrdersCustomerIdIndex.cs

Captured output: page query = Limit > Index Scan using IX_orders_customer_id_id, Index Cond (customer_id = 7) AND (id > 120000), actual rows=20, no Sort; count(*) customer 7 = Aggregate > Index Only Scan, Index Cond (customer_id = 7), rows=2000.

Captured output: inside BEGIN..ROLLBACK with IX_orders_customer_id_id dropped and IX_orders_customer_id recreated, the page query plan is Limit > Index Scan using PK_orders, Index Cond (id > 120000), Filter (customer_id = 7), Rows Removed by Filter: 1966.

With only a customer_id index and the primary key, the alternative plan for the page is Limit > Sort (top-N) > Bitmap Heap Scan via the customer_id index with Filter id > 120000; on donhang_perf the planner prices it higher than the PK walk.

claims.text: An Index Only Scan can answer from the index entries alone; table rows are visited only when the visibility map requires it, and Heap Fetches counts those visits (0 here, so no table rows were read).
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 11.9 Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes; 14.1 Using EXPLAIN

claims.text: PostgreSQL DDL is transactional: DROP INDEX and CREATE INDEX inside BEGIN are undone by ROLLBACK.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: BEGIN / ROLLBACK reference; db/queries/composite-index.sql:28-29 comment; captured output

claims.text: On donhang_perf, EXPLAIN of a query filtering on id alone (WHERE id = 120086) uses Index Scan on PK_orders.

Try it: with LIMIT 100 the first plan is Limit (actual rows=100 loops=1) > Index Scan using IX_orders_customer_id_id (actual rows=100 loops=1), same Index Cond, no Sort (customer 7 has 800 orders after id 120000).

claims.text: Keeping the single-column index next to the composite one adds work to every write for little or no gain: each insert must add an entry to every index on the table.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: 11.1 Introduction ('keep it synchronized with the table ... overhead to data manipulation'; remove seldom-used indexes)

claims.text: The page query in composite-index.sql is the inner SELECT of the SQL EF Core sends for ListByCustomerAsync, with parameters filled in.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement and prints actual rows and loops; COSTS/TIMING/SUMMARY OFF hide estimates, per-node times and total times. Index Cond is checked against index entries (here it bounds the scan); Filter is applied to each row read, Rows Removed by Filter counts failures.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs: EXPLAIN reference (ANALYZE, COSTS, TIMING); 14.1.1-14.1.2 Using EXPLAIN (Index Cond vs Filter, Rows Removed by Filter)
